headline: Longshots (odds of 15 or more) win 2.4% of the time against 0.1% implied by the odds, so they win more often than the market says.

metrics.label: Average market margin
metrics.explanation: How much the raw implied chances add up to above 100 percent, shown as a share of the total.

metrics.label: Short odds win rate
metrics.explanation: Actual win rate against the margin-free implied rate for runners with odds under 5.

metrics.label: Long odds win rate
metrics.explanation: Actual win rate against the margin-free implied rate for runners with odds of 15 or more.

metrics.label: Calibration slope
metrics.explanation: 1.00 means odds are perfectly calibrated. Below 1 means the market overrates longshots relative to favorites.

findings.statement: Longshots and favorites are not priced equally fairly.
findings.evidence: Long odds runners win 2.4% against 0.1% implied. Short odds runners win 21.5% against 1.2% implied.
findings.so_what: Review the price of the bands with the biggest gap first, because that is where price and result differ most.

findings.statement: A flat bet on every runner returns different amounts in different odds groups.
findings.evidence: Betting 1 unit on every runner returns -31.6% overall, -38.3% on short odds and -31.4% on long odds.
findings.so_what: Use return per unit staked by odds group as a simple monthly pricing health metric.

findings.statement: The calibration regression shows how far the odds are from fair.
findings.evidence: The slope is 0.73 (standard error 0.01) where 1.00 is perfect. 0 odds bands look too harsh and 8 too generous out of 8 bands, using 95 percent intervals.
findings.so_what: Track the slope over time and by track. A falling slope would signal growing longshot bias.

findings.evidence: For long odds runners, S has the lowest gap (+1.1 points, 25,822 runners) and HV has the highest (+2.8 points, 39,516 runners).
findings.so_what: Focus commercial review on the tracks with the biggest gaps and check them against competitor prices.

method_notes.why: Grouping runners into odds bands and counting wins gives a direct actual versus implied comparison.
method_notes.alternative: A plain scatter of every runner was not used because each point is only a win or a loss and shows nothing.

method_notes.why: Splitting by track, race class and odds group shows where prices are off, not only whether they are off overall.
method_notes.alternative: One overall number was not used because it hides local gaps. Very small segments are dropped to avoid noise.

method_notes.why: Regressing win on the log-odds of the implied chance gives one slope that summarises bias. Runners in the same race are linked, so errors are clustered by race.
method_notes.alternative: A simple correlation or a chi-square test was not used because they do not say which direction the bias runs.

caveats: Final odds (winning_odds) are assumed to be decimal odds that include the returned stake, so the implied chance is 1 divided by the odds.
Implied chances are scaled to add to 100 percent in each race, which removes the bookmaker margin before comparing.
Runners with missing or zero odds were removed as non-runners. A runner that truly started but has no price would slightly distort its race.
Priced runners with no numeric placing (for example pulled up) count as non-winners.
Dead heats count as wins for each horse involved, which slightly raises win rates.
Track means the race_location column and race type means the race_class column. Other race details were not used.
Data was scraped from public websites and the license is not stated, so check reuse terms before sharing.
This covers pool-style racing markets. It cannot show how FanDuel or competitors price the same races.
Bands marked too harsh or too generous are statistical signals on past races, not proof of future gaps.
